title: Hinduism: the act, not the fruit
hookLine: Krishna tells Arjuna to act without clinging to results (Bhagavad Gita 2.47)

lines: A MAN WHO CAN'T LIFT HIS BOW.
cards: You send the job application, then check your email forty times. You post the thing, then watch the likes. You cook for someone, then study their face on the first bite.
The work was done an hour ago, but your mind is still stuck on what comes back.
The Bhagavad Gita, a Hindu scripture, has a line about exactly this, spoken on a battlefield to a man so frozen by consequences he can't lift his bow. The path it points to is called karma yoga.

teach.b: The Gita is set at the edge of a great battle in the epic Mahabharata. The warrior Arjuna looks across the field and sees his own cousins, teachers and elders on the other side. He drops his bow and says he won't fight.
His charioteer is Krishna, whom Hindus revere as God come to earth, and their conversation makes up the whole Gita.

teach.h: A RIGHT TO THE ACT, NOT THE FRUIT.
teach.b: In chapter two, verse forty-seven, Krishna says, roughly: you have a right to your action, but never to its fruits. Don't let the fruit be your reason for acting, and don't let that turn you toward doing nothing, either.
That's karma yoga. Karma here simply means action, what you do. Yoga is traced to a root meaning to yoke, to join: a discipline, a path.
So karma yoga is the path of action: doing your work fully while letting go of your grip on how it turns out. Krishna doesn't say results don't matter, or that you shouldn't care.

teach.h: DO IT FULLY, THEN OPEN YOUR HAND.
teach.b: The doing is yours; the outcome isn't in your hands, so don't chain yourself to it. Later in the Gita, he adds that whatever a person does can be offered to him, as worship.
Hindus read this battlefield in more than one way. Some take it as a real war and a warrior's real duty. Others, Mahatma Gandhi among them, read it as the struggle inside every person.
Either way, the line fits a weekday at a desk. Do the task. Do it well.

how: Hindus who follow karma yoga treat it as a way of daily life: doing one's work and duties carefully, often offering them to God, without clinging to the results.

o: doing your work fully, without clinging to how it turns out
a series of physical poses practiced to calm a busy mind
a vow of silence kept until a wish comes true

games.q: you're Arjuna. your own family stands across the field. you've dropped your bow. what does Krishna tell you?
o: go home; nothing is worth this.
act, and let go of clinging to the fruits.
fight only if you're sure to win.
games.why: Krishna tells him he has a right to the action, never to its fruits, and not to turn toward doing nothing either. that's karma yoga.

practice: Pick one thing you'll do after this, an email, a meal, a conversation, and picture yourself doing it fully, with care, as well as you can.
Then picture the moment it's done, and open your actual hand, palm up, letting the result go wherever it goes.

wordCard.voice: Karma yoga. The path of action: do your work fully, and let go of clinging to its fruits, as Krishna tells Arjuna in the Gita. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the path, or discipline, of action.

carryVoice: Your line: the act, not the fruit. The doing can be enough. See you tomorrow.
